title: Current and potential difference — the basics of every circuit
examTip: Questions using Q = It, E = QV and R = V/I come up almost every year. I-V characteristics are a favourite for 'describe and explain' questions, especially the filament lamp and diode. Examiners want the physics reason, not just the shape.
introTips: This covers electric current, potential difference and resistance. These are the three quantities used in every electricity question
You will practise rearranging Q = It, E = QV and R = V/I to find any unknown
By the end, you will be able to sketch and explain I-V graphs for three different components. You will also be able to describe the required practical
intro: Every electrical device you have used works because charge flows around a circuit and transfers energy. That includes your phone, a kettle and Christmas lights. Current, potential difference and resistance let you predict exactly how any circuit will behave. Those three ideas come up on almost every electricity paper. Get them right, and a big chunk of this topic becomes simple.

basics.text: Electric charge is what flows when electricity flows. In a metal wire, tiny charged particles can move along the wire. You cannot see charge, but you can see what it does, like lighting a bulb.
A circuit is a complete loop of wire that charge can flow round. It is like a running track: you end up back where you started. If there is a gap anywhere, nothing flows.
A cell is what pushes charge round a circuit. A battery is two or more cells joined together. It is a bit like a pump pushing water round a loop of pipe.
Energy is what is needed to make things happen. It makes things move, heat up, light up or make a sound. You cannot see energy, but you can see what it does.
A rate tells you how much happens each second. Speed is a rate: how many metres you travel each second.
Letters in an equation stand for quantities, such as t for time. Two letters written side by side are multiplied together. To use it, swap the letters for numbers.

basics.idea: The two axes of a graph
basics.text: A graph has a line across the bottom, called the x-axis. The line up the side is the y-axis. Each one shows a quantity you measured. Each point on the graph is one pair of readings.
The origin is the corner of a graph where both axes start at zero. A line "through the origin" starts from that corner. It means that when one quantity is zero, so is the other.

keyPoints.heading: Electric current — charge on the move
keyPoints.content: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge. Charge is measured in coulombs (C) and current in amperes (A). The equation linking them is Q = It. Here Q is charge flow (C), I is current (A) and t is time (s). So 1 ampere means 1 coulomb of charge passes a point every second. Charge only flows through a closed circuit that includes a source of potential difference, such as a cell. In a single closed loop, the current has the same value at every point.
writeBullets: Electric current — the rate of flow of charge (coulombs per second)
Ampere (A) — the unit of current. 1 ampere is 1 coulomb per second
Q = It — charge flow (C) = current (A) × time (s)
Closed circuit — charge only flows if the circuit includes a source of potential difference
Single closed loop — the current is the same at every point
Ammeter — measures current. Always connected in series

keyTerms.def: Rate of flow of electric charge, measured in amperes (A)
The unit of electric charge (C); 1 coulomb = 1 ampere × 1 second

keyPoints.memTip: Q = It: 'Quiet Is Time'. Charge = current × time.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Charge only flows in a closed circuit with a source of potential difference. In a single loop, the current is the same everywhere.

keyPoints.heading: Potential difference — the energy push
keyPoints.content: Potential difference (p.d.) is measured in volts. It tells you how much energy is transferred for each coulomb of charge that flows between two points. Work is done when charge flows in a circuit. The equation is E = QV. Here E is energy transferred (joules, J), Q is charge flow (coulombs, C) and V is potential difference (volts, V). A p.d. of 1 volt means 1 joule of energy is transferred for every 1 coulomb of charge that passes.
writeBullets: Potential difference (p.d.) — energy transferred per unit charge. Measured in volts (V)
E = QV — energy transferred (J) = charge flow (C) × potential difference (V)
1 volt — 1 joule of energy per 1 coulomb of charge
Voltmeter — measures p.d. Always connected in parallel

keyTerms.def: Energy transferred per coulomb of charge between two points; measured in volts (V)

keyPoints.memTip: E = QV: energy transferred = charge flow × potential difference. More charge or a bigger p.d. means more energy.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Potential difference is about energy per coulomb. A bigger p.d. means each coulomb transfers more energy.

keyPoints.heading: Resistance — the opposition to current
keyPoints.content: Resistance is the opposition to the flow of current. The greater the resistance, the less current flows for a given potential difference. The equation linking the three is V = IR (potential difference = current × resistance). It works for any component. Rearranged, R = V/I. Here R is resistance in ohms (Ω), V is potential difference in volts, and I is current in amperes. For example, say the p.d. across a resistor is 12 V and the current through it is 3 A. Then R = 12/3 = 4 Ω. Or if V = 12 V and R = 4 Ω, then I = V/R = 12/4 = 3 A. Resistance increases with the length of the wire. A hotter wire, such as a filament, has more resistance. A thermistor's resistance decreases as it gets hotter. Required practical. In this required practical you investigate how the length of a wire affects its resistance, at constant temperature. Measure V and I, then work out R = V/I. You also measure the resistance of resistors combined in series and in parallel.
writeBullets: Resistance — opposition to current. Measured in ohms (Ω)
R = V/I — resistance = potential difference ÷ current. It rearranges to V = IR and I = V/R
Ohmic conductor — R is constant at constant temperature (current ∝ potential difference)
Length — longer wire → greater resistance
Temperature — a hotter filament has more resistance. A hotter thermistor has less
A required practical — measure R for different lengths of wire, and for resistors in series and in parallel

keyTerms.def: Opposition to the flow of electric current; measured in ohms (Ω)
The unit of resistance; 1 ohm is 1 volt per ampere

keyPoints.memTip: R = V/I: use the triangle. Put V on top, and I and R on the bottom. Cover any one to get the formula.
keyPoints.tutor_note: In calculations, always write the formula first. Then substitute values, then calculate. Showing your working gets method marks, even if your arithmetic slips.

keyPoints.heading: I-V characteristics — how components really behave
keyPoints.content: An I-V characteristic graph shows how current changes with potential difference for a component. Current (I) goes on the y-axis and potential difference (V) on the x-axis. An ohmic conductor (for example, a fixed resistor at constant temperature) gives a straight line through the origin. Doubling V doubles I, so resistance is constant. This graph is linear. A filament lamp gives a curve that flattens as V increases. As the current rises, the filament heats up and its resistance increases. So the graph curves away from the straight line. A diode only lets current flow in one direction (the forward direction). The diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction. So only a very small current flows. The filament lamp and diode graphs are non-linear. To find the resistance at any point, read off V and I. Then use R = V ÷ I. You need to know the shape AND the reason for it. Examiners will ask you to explain, not just describe.
writeBullets: I-V graph — current (y-axis) vs potential difference (x-axis) for a component
Ohmic conductor — straight line through the origin. Resistance is constant
Filament lamp — S-shaped curve. Resistance increases as temperature rises
Diode — conducts in one direction only. Very high resistance in the reverse direction, so a very small current
Linear — a straight-line graph (resistor at constant temperature). Non-linear — a curve (filament lamp, diode)
Resistance at a point on an I-V graph — read off V and I, then use R = V ÷ I

keyTerms.def: A graph of current against potential difference showing how a component behaves
A component whose resistance stays constant at constant temperature — gives a straight-line I-V graph
A component that allows current in one direction only; very high resistance in reverse

keyPoints.memTip: Three shapes: straight line = resistor. Bendy S = lamp (it gets hot). One-sided hockey stick = diode (one direction only). Cover your notes and sketch all three graphs with labels from memory.
keyPoints.tutor_note: A very common mistake is drawing the filament lamp curve the wrong way. It should curve AWAY from the straight line, not towards the I-axis. That is because resistance increases, so less current flows than a simple proportion would give. A diode does not block all current in the reverse direction. Its resistance is very high, so a very small current flows.

keyPoints.heading: Required practical — measuring I-V characteristics
keyPoints.content: The required practical asks you to measure I-V characteristics. You test a filament lamp, a diode and a resistor at constant temperature. The circuit uses: - a variable resistor (rheostat) to change the current - an ammeter in series with the component to measure I - a voltmeter in parallel with the component to measure V Record pairs of I and V values as you adjust the variable resistor. Then plot the I-V graph. To get both positive and negative V on the graph, turn the component round. Or swap the battery connections. Safety: filament lamps get very hot, so do not touch the bulb. Keep currents within the given limits so components don't overheat. Always start with the variable resistor at maximum resistance (minimum current) before switching on.
writeBullets: Ammeter — placed in series with the component to measure the current through it
Voltmeter — placed in parallel across the component to measure the p.d. across it
Variable resistor — used to change the current in the circuit and collect many data points
Reverse connections — swap the battery or component to get negative V values and complete the I-V curve
Safety — start at max resistance. The lamp gets very hot. Stay within current limits
Repeats — take repeat readings and average them to reduce random error

keyTerms.def: A resistor whose resistance can be changed — used to vary the current in a circuit
Instrument measuring current; connected in series
Instrument measuring p.d.; connected in parallel

keyPoints.memTip: Series A, Parallel V: Ammeter in Series, Voltmeter in Parallel. Cover your notes. Describe the full circuit from memory, including the safety step.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Examiners often ask why each meter goes where it does. The voltmeter is in parallel because it must measure the p.d. across the component. The ammeter is in series to measure the same current that flows through the component. Know the reason, not just the rule.

0.question: A charge of 60 C passes through a component in 20 s. What is the current?
0.correctFeedback: Correct. I = Q/t = 60/20 = 3 A. You rearranged Q = It perfectly.
0.wrongFeedback: Rearrange Q = It to I = Q/t. Divide the charge (60 C) by the time (20 s): 60 ÷ 20 = 3 A. Watch out for multiplying instead of dividing, or mixing up the letters.

1.question: A charge flow of 5 C moves through a potential difference of 12 V. How much energy is transferred?
1.wrongFeedback: Use E = QV (energy transferred = charge flow × potential difference). E = 5 C × 12 V = 60 J.

2.question: A lamp has a p.d. of 12 V across it and a current of 0.5 A through it. What is its resistance at this moment?
2.correctFeedback: Correct. R = V/I = 12 ÷ 0.5 = 24 Ω. Well done for using R = V/I and dividing by a decimal.
2.wrongFeedback: Use R = V/I. Substitute: R = 12 ÷ 0.5 = 24 Ω. Dividing by 0.5 is the same as multiplying by 2, so 12 × 2 = 24 Ω. If you chose 6 Ω, you probably divided by 2 instead of 0.5.

3.question: Which of these best explains why the I-V graph for a filament lamp curves, rather than being straight?
options: The lamp only conducts in one direction
As current increases, the filament heats up, which increases its resistance
The lamp's potential difference decreases as current increases
The ammeter reads incorrectly at high currents
3.correctFeedback: Exactly right. The filament heats up and its resistance rises. So the current is lower than a simple proportion would give. That causes the curve.
3.wrongFeedback: The key physics here is temperature. As more current flows, the filament gets hotter. In a metal, a higher temperature means more resistance. So each extra volt gives less extra current than before. That makes the graph curve.

4.question: In the I-V required practical, how should the ammeter and voltmeter be connected?
options: Ammeter in series with the component, voltmeter in parallel across it
Both in series with the component
Both in parallel across the component
Ammeter in parallel, voltmeter in series
4.correctFeedback: Correct. The ammeter is in series to measure the current through the component. The voltmeter is in parallel to measure the p.d. across it.
4.wrongFeedback: The ammeter must be in series, so the same current flows through it and the component. The voltmeter must be in parallel, to measure the p.d. across the component.

commonMistakes: Drawing the filament lamp I-V curve bending towards the I-axis instead of away from it. It curves away because resistance increases, so less current flows than expected.
Connecting the voltmeter in series instead of parallel. A voltmeter must be in parallel to measure the p.d. across a component without changing the current.
Forgetting to check units in Q = It. Time must be in seconds, not minutes or hours, before substituting.
Saying a diode 'blocks all current' in the reverse direction. It has a very high resistance, so a very small current flows.
examTips: Always show the formula, then the substitution, then the answer with units. Even one mark is at stake if you skip a step.

For 'describe and explain' I-V questions, name the shape and then explain the physics. For example: 'The curve means resistance is increasing, because the filament temperature rises as current increases'.

In the required practical, know why each meter goes where it does. Don't just say 'ammeter = series, voltmeter = parallel'. Give the reason. The ammeter measures the current through the component. The voltmeter measures the p.d. across it.
Current is only directly proportional to potential difference for an ohmic conductor at constant temperature. Don't assume this for lamps or diodes.
revisionCardBullets: Current (I) — the rate of flow of charge. Unit: ampere (A)
Q = It — charge flow (C) = current (A) × time (s)
Potential difference (V) — energy per unit charge. Unit: volt (V)
E = QV — energy transferred (J) = charge flow (C) × potential difference (V)
R = V/I — resistance (Ω) = potential difference ÷ current
Ohmic conductor — constant resistance. Straight-line I-V graph through the origin
Filament lamp — resistance increases with temperature. Curved I-V graph
Diode — conducts in one direction only. Very high resistance in the reverse direction
Ammeter goes in series. Voltmeter goes in parallel
